summary: A classroom-style fictional dialogue in which a teacher argues that the Constitution is a living document and that the Framers, fleeing tyranny, wrote the Bill of Rights to guarantee absolute rights against future government overreach. She ties the role of government to securing life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, in that order, and justifies some limits on liberty by appeal to protecting life. Students, including the narrator, push back, asking whether national security could justify suspending the Bill of Rights, and the excerpt ends mid-argument.
one_line: Excerpt from a fictional Book 1 classroom debate over the Constitution as a living document, the Bill of Rights, and whether life outweighs liberty.
key_facts: The teacher argues the framers of the Constitution intended it to be a living document that was revised over time.
The teacher says the framers never intended the Constitution to be looked on like religious doctrine.
The narrator says the framers were merchants and artisans who were loyal to the King until he instituted policies against their interests.
The teacher says the Bill of Rights is not supposed to be something you pick and choose from.
The teacher says what the Framers hated was tyranny, and the Bill of Rights is supposed to prevent it.
The phrase "Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" is written on the board by the teacher.
The teacher says the framers set out the Bill of Rights because having absolute rights was better than the risk that someone would take them away.
The teacher uses the First Amendment as an example, saying it prevents the government from creating allowed speech and criminal speech.
The teacher states that the role of government is to secure for citizens the rights of life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, in that order.
The teacher describes the order of rights as a filter, saying liberty and happiness may be reduced to protect life.
The teacher uses police power to lock up people who are a danger to themselves or others as an example of losing liberty to protect life.
A student asks whether this means the government can do anything it wants if it says it is stopping someone from hurting us in the future.
A student says the argument sounds like national security is more important than the Constitution.
The narrator asks, "How can you protect freedom by suspending the Bill of Rights?"
The teacher shakes her head at the students as if they were being very stupid, and the excerpt ends mid-sentence with the word "revolutionary".
